extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and readers interested in poetic theory and composition; aspiring lyric/ballad writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing lyrical/ballad poetry that uses the language of ordinary people and subjects from common or rural life, emphasising truthful description, emotional authenticity, and measured metrical craft. Includes what to choose as subject, how to handle diction and metre, and the compositional mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make incidents of common life interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal object ... was to make the incidents of common life interesting by tracing in them, truly though not ostentatiously, the primary laws of our nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain and exemplify human feelings by following the 'fluxes and refluxes of the mind' when agitated by great and simple affections. Use examples like the IDIOT BOY, the MAD MOTHER, the FORSAKEN INDIAN, WE ARE SEVEN, and SIMON LEE to show how ordinary incidents can yield important moral and psychological insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose low and rustic life as appropriate subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Low and rustic life was generally chosen because in that situation the essential passions of the heart find a better soil ... are less under restraint, and speak a plainer and more emphatic language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer characters and occupations where elementary feelings exist with simplicity and durability; rural manners germinate from elementary feelings and link naturally with the beautiful and permanent forms of nature. Such choice makes passions more accessible and more profitably contemplated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the real language of men in vivid sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitting to metrical arrangement a selection of the real language of men in a state of vivid sensation ... to imitate, and, as far as possible, to adopt the very language of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language arising from repeated experience and regular feelings, purified of real defects but not artificially ornamented. Because common people, less subject to social vanity, convey feelings in simple, unelaborated expressions, their speech is a more permanent and philosophical source for poetic diction (cf. Chaucer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Each poem should have a worthy purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: From such verses the Poems in these volumes will be found distinguished at least by one mark of difference, that each of them has a worthy 'purpose'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems should not be mere verbal display; they should aim to illuminate human nature, associations of ideas, or moral truths. Even when not begun with a formal purpose, good poems should show a purpose derived from sustained thought and meditation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the conventional 'poetic diction' and overused phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: There will also be found in these volumes little of what is usually called poetic diction; I have taken as much pains to avoid it as others ordinarily take to produce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from inherited poetical phrases and figures repeated by bad poets; restrict expressions that have become foolishly repeated and connected with disgust. Favor plainness and fitness of language to the idea's importance rather than inherited 'poetic' ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personifications of abstract ideas (except sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in a very few instances the Reader will find no personifications of abstract ideas in these volumes ... they may be well fitted for certain sorts of composition, but in these Poems I propose ... to adopt the very language of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit allegorical or personified abstractions because they are not part of natural speech; keep the reader among 'flesh and blood' characters to preserve interest and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metre for balance and tempering of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction of rhyme and metre is regular and uniform ... the metre obeys certain laws ... which cannot but have great efficacy in tempering and restraining the passion by an intertexture of ordinary feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in verse when metre can provide regular impulses that temper powerful emotion and keep excitement within pleasurable bounds. Do not assume metre requires artificial poetic diction; metre itself can heighten pleasure and regulate passion when used with manly style and fitting subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce excitement accompanied by an overbalance of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Poetry is to produce excitement in coexistence with an overbalance of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conveying powerful or painful passions, ensure the reader's experience still leans toward pleasure (metre, harmonious language, the sense of difficulty overcome, and associations with prior pleasurable experiences help achieve this). Examples: Shakespeare tempers pathos so it stays within pleasure's bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose from 'emotion recollected in tranquillity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful composition generally begins when an emotion is contemplated calmly so it can be re-experienced in controlled form; writers should think long and deeply so feeling becomes modified and directed by thought, producing more lasting and illuminating poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit prose-like lines when appropriate; prosaisms are not automatically faults
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a Poem there should be found a series of lines, or even a single line, in which the language, though naturally arranged and according to the strict laws of metre, does not differ from that of prose ... these prosaisms ... are not necessarily defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject lines as flawed simply because they resemble good prose; many valuable poetic passages are prose-like in diction when prose itself is well written (Gray example). Judge by effect and truth, not by a dogmatic separation of prose and verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid triviality and meanness of thought or language
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot be insensible of the present outcry against the triviality and meanness both of thought and language ... this defect ... is more dishonorable to the Writer's own character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure subject-matter has sense and the capacity to lead to something interesting; parody comparison (Dr. Johnson stanza vs Babes in the Wood) shows similar diction can be admirable or contemptible depending on the matter. Decide genus (is subject interesting?) before arguing about species (whether it's poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for truthfulness and 'little falsehood of description'
rubrics_metrics.description: I have at all times endeavoured to look steadily at my subject, consequently I hope it will be found that there is in these Poems little falsehood of description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe objects and persons with fidelity; avoid exaggerated or false images. Accuracy of observation contributes to the poet's good sense and the work's lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ the principle of 'similitude in dissimilitude' to give pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the chief of these causes is ... the pleasure which the mind derives from the perception of similitude in dissimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unexpected but illuminating analogies and contrasts (similitude amid dissimilitude) to stimulate intellectual pleasure and enrich imagery; though Wordsworth does not fully develop it here, he marks it as a key source of poetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop feelings by long meditation and intellectual habit
rubrics_metrics.description: All good poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings; but ... Poems to which any value can be attached, were never produced ... but by a man who being possessed of more than usual organic sensibility had also thought long and deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate habits of meditation so feelings are modified and directed by thought; repeated contemplation leads to significant, controlled expression rather than impulsive or superficial emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not alter expressions merely to placate critics; preserve authorial conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is dangerous to make these alterations on the simple authority of a few individuals ... for his own feelings are his stay and support ... he may be induced to repeat this act till his mind loses all confidence in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise when the author is genuinely convinced a change improves the work, not simply to avoid criticism. Guard against eroding one's artistic instincts by surrendering to external opinion alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek to affect the reader's genuine feelings rather than appeal to social judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: I request that the Reader would abide independently by his own feelings, and that if he finds himself affected he would not suffer such conjectures to interfere with his pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write and arrange poems to produce authentic emotional responses in readers. Avoid composing for how classes of people 'will appear' to judge the work; instead, aim for directness of effect on an individual reader's sensibilities.
